composition.story: A tokenizer splits a word into characters, then applies learned merge rules in a fixed rank order. Each rule joins one adjacent pair wherever it appears. When no rule applies, each piece is looked up for an integer ID. Compare "lower" with "lowest": both keep the shared piece "low" with the same ID; only the suffix differs.

aha.observation: In both words, "low" becomes ID 312. Only the suffix changes: "er" is 263 and "est" is 478. Joining the pieces gives back the original text.

parts.presentation: Top row of state labels. The current state is highlighted, and completed states show the trace.
Regions from left to right: input text, merge rules, current pieces, vocabulary, token IDs. Regions named in state.active are highlighted.
Anchored to the active region. Says where the change happens and why.
Faint outline of the regions highlighted in the previous state, so the learner can see the before and after of each merge.
Status line under the picture showing pieces, piece count, rules applied and the rejoined text. Each value appears here only.

controls.label: Step
controls.presentation: Previous and Next buttons with fixed names. At the first and last states, the buttons are disabled but keep their names. Keyboard arrows work, and focus is visible.

controls.label: Input word
controls.presentation: Changes the input word, which changes the variant. It is the only parameter control. The merge rules and vocabulary stay the same.

controls.label: Reset
controls.presentation: Returns to the first state with the word set to "lower".

states.label: Split
states.sentence: The word "lower" is split into five single characters.
states.why: Merging starts from the smallest units, which are single characters.

states.label: Rule 1
states.sentence: Rule 1 finds the pair l+o and joins it into lo.
states.why: Rules are tried in rank order, so the most frequent pair goes first.

states.label: Rule 2
states.sentence: Rule 2 joins lo+w into low, an earlier merge being reused.
states.why: Merges build on each other, so longer pieces grow from shorter ones.

states.label: Rule 3
states.why: The pair e+r appears here, so the rule fires.

states.label: No match
states.sentence: Rules 4 and 5 find no e+s or es+t pair, so merging stops.
states.why: A rule changes the pieces only when its exact pair is present.

states.label: IDs
states.sentence: Each piece is looked up, so low becomes 312 and er becomes 263.
states.why: The model reads integer IDs, never raw letters.

states.label: Split
states.sentence: The word "lowest" is split into six single characters.
states.why: Merging starts from the smallest units, which are single characters.

states.label: Rule 1
states.sentence: Rule 1 joins l+o into lo, the same as in "lower".
states.why: The same rules run in the same order for every word.

states.label: Rule 2
states.sentence: Rule 2 joins lo+w into low, making the shared prefix piece.

states.label: Rule 3 skipped
states.sentence: Rule 3 finds no e+r pair, so nothing changes.
states.why: A rule fires only when its exact pair is present.

states.label: Rule 4
states.why: The suffix is now built from the pairs this word actually contains.

states.label: Rule 5
states.sentence: Rule 5 joins es+t into est, and no rules remain.
states.why: Merging ends after the last ranked rule.

states.label: IDs
states.sentence: Each piece is looked up: low is 312 again, and est is 478.
states.why: Shared pieces get identical IDs, so the model sees what related words have in common.

1.reason: The pipeline from text through merges to IDs, compared across lower and lowest, answers how shared pieces get shared IDs.

2.reason: The aha state "ids" is the final state of both variants, and stepping is manual, so it holds until the learner acts.

3.reason: The word select changes the pieces, the rule path (rule 3 skipped, rules 4 and 5 fired), the suffix ID and the counts, while the rules and vocabulary stay fixed.

4.reason: Callouts, highlights, ghosts and readouts all bind to state fields and declared regions and links, though the phase-to-state mapping is implicit.

6.reason: The story, state sentences, labels and readouts consistently name the same rules, pieces and IDs.

7.reason: Balanced depth shows five purposeful regions, one callout and a four-value readout, within the density ceiling.

8.reason: The piece counts, rules-applied counts and rejoined text are correct at every state, including the skipped rule, and each value appears once in the readouts.
